analysis.one_liner: Bans political action committees from federal elections and halves the individual contribution limit.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 1992, referred to the House Administration Committee, and never received a vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have banned political action committees — the pooled-money committees funded by corporations, unions, and trade associations — from spending or raising money in federal elections. It would also cut the individual contribution limit to candidates from $1,000 to $500. It never got past its first referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want campaigns funded by small individual donors rather than pooled special-interest committees, and candidates who raise money from individuals rather than PAC networks.

how_it_helps.text: It would prohibit political action committees from soliciting or receiving contributions or making expenditures in federal elections, removing a channel through which organized money interests fund congressional campaigns [S2][S3].
It would cut the maximum an individual could give to a candidate from $1,000 to $500, shrinking the weight of any single large donation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: PACs funded by corporations, unions, and trade associations, and members of Congress whose campaigns currently draw large shares of money from those committees.

drawbacks.text: A ban on PAC money would not eliminate big money in politics; large donors could still give to parties, and the bill offers no replacement funding such as public financing, so candidates may become even more dependent on wealthy individuals [S2][S3].

Cutting the individual limit to $500 could leave grassroots-funded candidates with less to spend against self-funded or independently backed opponents, since the bill addresses PAC spending but not independent expenditures by individuals [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — cutting special-interest committee money out of federal campaigns — directly serves voters, but the bill is a blunt instrument with no public-financing substitute, so its practical effect on who really funds campaigns is uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Administration Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Romano Mazzoli introduced the bill on April 9, 1992, joined by four Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on House Administration, which is where campaign-finance legislation begins in the House [S1][S5].
No further action was taken before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, so the bill died in committee [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs and the corporate, union, and trade-association interests that fund them — their role in congressional campaigns was untouched, and incumbents continue to collect PAC money.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PACs and the interests that fund them

for.name: Rep. Romano L. Mazzoli
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban PAC activity in federal elections and lower the individual contribution limit.

for.name: Reps. Glenn Poshard, Robert Atkins, Andrew Jacobs, and Mike Synar

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral for campaign-finance bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record, and the committee that buried it was chaired by a Democrat in a Democratic-majority House.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, union, and trade-association PACs)
industries.note: The bill would have banned PACs from soliciting, receiving, or spending money in federal elections, ending their channel into congressional campaigns. PACs profit their sponsors by giving them outsized access to lawmakers, which runs against voters' interest in campaigns funded by ordinary citizens.

A PAC ban and a lower individual limit would shrink the market for PAC fundraising and compliance services while pushing campaigns toward more numerous, smaller-donor appeals. The bill's death left this business untouched.
